analysis.one_liner: Caps pain-and-suffering awards in medical malpractice lawsuits at $250,000 and restricts patients' ability to sue.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 1993, sent to two House committees, and never received a hearing or a vote before the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set national rules for medical malpractice lawsuits, overriding state laws wherever the state rules favored patients. It capped compensation for pain and suffering at $250,000 no matter how bad the injury, cut the time patients have to sue, required patients to give doctors 90 days' warning before suing, reduced any award by whatever the patient already received from insurance or disability benefits, and limited lawyers' fees. It never received a committee vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Physicians, hospitals, and medical malpractice insurers. Damage caps, collateral-source offsets, shortened filing deadlines, and fee limits all reduce the size and number of malpractice claims against providers and the premiums insurers charge them. State medical societies also gain, since the bill would let them participate in reviewing malpractice claims against their own members with legal immunity for that review. Patients who are sued over... rather, doctors facing suits benefit directly; the bill's own findings describe litigation as driving up provider insurance premiums [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Capped noneconomic malpractice damages at $250,000 total per injury, regardless of how many parties were sued or how many claims were filed — the amount patients can recover for pain, suffering, disfigurement, and loss of enjoyment of life.

Required courts to reduce any award by amounts the patient already received or will receive from health insurance, disability programs, employer sick pay, or any other source (collateral-source offsets), so malpractice victims could effectively be paid twice by no one.
Shortened the time to sue: claims had to be filed within two years of when the injury reasonably should have been discovered, and never more than four years after the injury occurred.

Limited lawyers' contingency fees on a sliding scale from 40% down to 15%, reducing what claimants' attorneys could take and thereby making it less profitable for lawyers to take smaller malpractice cases.

Required 90 days' advance notice before filing a suit, allowed courts to order large future-damage awards paid in installments rather than up front, and let state medical societies participate in reviewing malpractice claims against their own members with legal immunity for that review.

analysis.who_pays: Patients injured by medical negligence. The cap on noneconomic damages applies even in catastrophic cases, and collateral-source offsets mean a patient whose insurer already paid medical bills could see the award reduced accordingly. Trial attorneys would also earn less on these cases, which in turn means fewer lawyers willing to take smaller malpractice claims.

drawbacks.text: The $250,000 cap on noneconomic damages applies no matter how severe the injury, so a patient left permanently disabled or disfigured by malpractice could collect nothing beyond medical bills and lost wages for that suffering — and the cap falls hardest on children, seniors, and stay-at-home parents who have little or no lost income to claim.

Mandatory offsets would reduce any award by every dollar the patient received from health insurance, disability programs, or employer benefits, meaning injured patients could repay or forfeit benefits they had already earned through premiums or work — a mechanism critics call the 'collateral source' giveaway to negligent providers and their insurers.

The two-year deadline running from when the injury 'should reasonably have been discovered,' with a four-year absolute cutoff, could bar claims by patients whose harm was hidden by their own doctor until it was too late to sue.
The bill would preempt stronger state consumer-protection laws, overriding any state that chose to give malpractice victims more generous damages or more time to sue.

The bill cites as its justification the claim that malpractice litigation drives up health care costs, but the CRS summary records this as a congressional finding rather than an established fact, and critics of damage caps have long argued the savings flow to insurers and providers rather than to patients' premiums.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill had a real rationale: malpractice suits and premiums raise health care costs, and California's similar cap is often credited with restraining premiums. But the costs fell entirely on patients: families whose child was catastrophically injured by malpractice would face the same $250,000 ceiling on pain-and-suffering damages as anyone else, collateral-source offsets could shrink awards to near zero for anyone with insurance, and the shortened deadlines risked time-barred claims. The trade-off was skewed toward lowering providers' insurance bills rather than compensating injured patients, and its federal preemption of state consumer protections was unusually sweeping.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to House subcommittees in the summer of 1993, no action was taken on it, and the record shows it was superseded by a different health bill the following summer; it never came to a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Dornan introduced the bill on June 16, 1993, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees.
Over the following month it was sent to three subcommittees — Economic and Commercial Law, Commerce/Consumer Protection, and Health and the Environment — where no markup or vote ever occurred.
On August 2, 1994, the action record lists the bill as 'See H.R.3600,' indicating its subject was absorbed into that separate health care bill; no floor action was ever taken on H.R. 2433 itself.
The bill had only 8 cosponsors, all Republicans, and no Democratic support in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Malpractice insurers, physicians, and their insurers are better off because the bill never became law is backwards — they would have gained if it passed; the outcome preserved patients' existing right to full compensation, while the insurers and provider interests lost the caps they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Patients; the caps doctors sought died

against.name: Plaintiffs' trial lawyers and consumer groups
against.what_they_did: Organized opposition to federal malpractice damage caps and fee limits during the 1993-94 health care debate; no opposition action on this specific bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: All 8 cosponsors were Republicans and the sponsor was a conservative Republican; no Democratic support appears in the record.

industries.note: Damage caps, fee limits, and offsets directly reduce claim payouts, which is the industry's core demand. The bill's own findings cite high malpractice premiums as the problem it solves.

Providers faced with malpractice suits would see their maximum liability drop sharply, since noneconomic damages are usually the largest component of malpractice awards. Their gain is funded by injured patients.
State medical societies could participate in reviewing malpractice claims against their own members with statutory immunity, embedding the profession in the process for judging itself.

Sliding-scale contingency fee caps cut the fees that fund malpractice litigation, reducing the number of cases lawyers can afford to take — which is precisely how the bill was designed to shrink lawsuits.
Mandatory collateral-source offsets shift costs from malpractice payouts onto the health insurance system, since patients' insurers would pay care costs that malpractice awards previously covered.
